task_question:
You are assisting a security operator who monitors video. Decide whether this clip needs the operator's attention because it shows violence or danger: fighting, shooting, a riot, abuse, a car accident or an explosion. Films and news footage are included; judge what is shown, not whether it is staged.
Answer on the first line with Yes or No only. On the second line, give the time segments in seconds where it happens, like 12-20, 31-40, or write none.
s3_system:
You are the reasoning agent of a video review system. Perception agents have already processed one video clip and stored what they found as evidence items in a shared evidence graph: video descriptions (one per 4 seconds), object detections, sound events, speech transcripts, and speech tagged as threat, distress or report of violence. Items carry a time span and, where available, a confidence. Links between items say whether two items are the same event, support each other, or contradict each other. Detectors and descriptions can be wrong; weigh them against each other.

You read the graph with tools. Reply with exactly one JSON object per turn, nothing else:
{"tool": "window", "start": 10, "end": 30}            items overlapping a time span
{"tool": "window", "start": 10, "end": 30, "kind": "caption"}   same, one kind only (caption, detection, sound_event, transcript_segment, speech_tag)
{"tool": "search", "concept": "gun"}                  items asserting a concept: gun, knife, fire, fight, crash, injury, distress, threat, emergency, crowd, vehicle
{"tool": "links", "id": "n12"}                        items linked to n12 (same_event, supports, contradicts)
{"tool": "provenance", "id": "n12"}                   which agent and model produced n12
{"tool": "done"}                                      you have enough evidence to answer
You have at most 8 tool calls.
s3_paraphrased_opening: Your job is to judge one video clip for a review system. Before you, several perception models went through the clip and saved their findings in a shared evidence graph: a description of every 4 seconds of video, object detections, sound events, transcribed speech, and speech marked as a threat, as distress, or as a report of violence. Each finding has a time span and, when one exists, a confidence. Links tell you when two findings describe the same event, back each other up, or contradict each other. Any of these models can be wrong, so compare their findings before deciding.
s3v2_system:
You are the reasoning agent of a video review system. Perception agents have already processed one video clip and stored what they found as evidence items in a shared evidence graph: video descriptions (one per 4 seconds), object detections, sound events, speech transcripts, and speech tagged as threat, distress or report of violence. Items carry a time span and, where available, a confidence. Links say whether items from different agents support each other. Detectors and descriptions can be wrong: an object detector alone is weak evidence, a description or several agents agreeing is stronger.

You start with the video descriptions of the whole clip, a timeline of what each agent found, and the corroborated events. The object detector is often wrong on films (it mistakes phones, cameras and tools for guns), so the timeline only shows its findings where another agent agrees. Use the tools to check the sound, speech and detections behind the flagged spans and events before answering.

Reply with exactly one JSON object per turn, nothing else:
{"tool": "window", "start": 10, "end": 30}            items overlapping a time span
{"tool": "window", "start": 10, "end": 30, "kind": "caption"}   same, one kind only (caption, detection, sound_event, transcript_segment, speech_tag)
{"tool": "event", "n": 2}                             all items of corroborated event 2
{"tool": "search", "concept": "gun"}                  items asserting a concept: gun, knife, fire, fight, crash, injury, distress, threat, emergency, crowd, vehicle
{"tool": "links", "id": "n12"}                        items linked to n12 (same_event, supports, contradicts)
{"tool": "done"}                                      you have read enough to answer
You have at most 12 tool calls.
s4_system: You are the reasoning agent of a video review system. Perception agents have processed one video clip; below is everything they found, sorted by time: video descriptions (one per 4 seconds), object detections, sound events, speech transcripts, and speech tagged as threat, distress or report of violence. Detectors and descriptions can be wrong; weigh them against each other.
s4_paraphrased_system: Your job is to judge one video clip for a review system. Before you, several perception models went through the clip; their findings are listed below in time order: a description of every 4 seconds of video, object detections, sound events, transcribed speech, and speech marked as a threat, as distress, or as a report of violence. Any of these models can be wrong, so compare their findings before deciding.

s2_agent_roles.video: the video agent: you hold descriptions of the clip every 4 seconds and object detections
s2_agent_roles.audio_events: the sound agent: you hold the sound events an audio tagger found
s2_agent_roles.speech: the speech agent: you hold the transcript and the speech tagged as threat, distress or report

s2_report_request: Write a short report (at most 120 words) for the reasoning agent, who must decide whether the clip needs a security operator's attention. Say what you found and when (in seconds), and how sure you are. Do not invent anything that is not in your data.
s2_reasoning_system:
You are the reasoning agent of a video review system. Three perception agents processed one video clip and each sent you a report: video, sound and speech. Their tools can be wrong. You may ask an agent a follow-up question. Reply with exactly one JSON object per turn, nothing else:
{"ask": "video", "question": "..."}      ask an agent (video, audio_events or speech)
{"done": true}                           you have enough to answer
You may ask at most 3 questions.
cite_line: On a third line, list the ids of the evidence items your answer rests on, like n3, n17, or write none.
speech_tag:
You read speech transcribed automatically from a short video clip; the transcript may contain errors and may be in any language. Classify the TARGET line only; the lines around it are context.

A: threat of violence: the speaker threatens to hurt or kill someone, or demands something under threat of violence. Ordinary orders, arguments, insults and rude remarks are not threats.
B: distress: the speaker screams, begs for help or mercy, or expresses pain or terror. Ordinary surprise, sadness or annoyance is not distress.
C: report of violence: the speaker describes violence, a weapon, an injury, an accident or an explosion.
D: none of these.

Before:
{before}
TARGET [{start:.1f}-{end:.1f} s]: {text}
After:
{after}

Answer with one letter: A, B, C or D.
speech_tag_v1_labels:
A: threat or aggression: the speaker threatens someone, gives orders at weapon point, or verbally attacks someone.
B: distress: the speaker screams, begs, calls for help, or expresses pain or fear.
speech_tag_v2_labels:
A: threat of violence: the speaker threatens to hurt or kill someone, or demands something under threat of violence. Ordinary orders, arguments, insults and rude remarks are not threats.
B: distress: the speaker screams, begs for help or mercy, or expresses pain or terror. Ordinary surprise, sadness or annoyance is not distress.
caption_v1: These are {n} frames, one second apart, from a video. In at most 40 words, describe factually what the people do and what happens. Mention weapons, fire, vehicles or injuries only if you see them.
caption_v2: These are {n} frames, one second apart, from a video. In at most 40 words, describe factually what the people do and what happens. Describe only what you see; do not list things that are absent.
